Gārgī, the sky-world is the limit of the measured, the end of the knowable, and the resting place of the unmeasured. Gārgī said: "Venerable Sir, that [sky-world] itself rests upon something else; it does not rest upon itself. Yājñavalkya said: "Gārgī, do not question beyond Brahman, lest your head shatter apart. Gārgī, Brahman is the limit of the measured, the end of the knowable, and the resting place of the unmeasured. Gārgī said: "Venerable Sir, I have asked about Brahman, and you have answered me about Brahman. Now I shall ask you about something else. Yājñavalkya said: "Ask, O Gārgī. Gārgī said: "Venerable Sir, as a man here, bound by a cord, goes eastward or westward to serve his master, so indeed do these worlds go toward Brahman as their master. Brahman is the lord of these worlds, Brahman is their king. Yājñavalkya said: "This is true, O Gārgī. But regarding that very Brahman, tell me—across what is this woven, warp and woof? Gārgī said: "Venerable Sir, across space (*ākāśa*) is this woven, warp and woof. Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, Gārgī, it is across space that this world, the other world, and all beings are woven, warp and woof. Verily, Gārgī, space is the unmanifest, the immortal, the manifest, and the mortal, the founded and the unfounded, the measured and the unmeasured, the defined and the undefined, the becoming and the non-becoming. But across what is space itself woven, warp and woof? Gārgī said: "Venerable Sir, my intellect has reached its limit; I am unable to answer further. Yājñavalkya said: "Gārgī, you have questioned beyond the domain of questioning; therefore, your head shall not shatter apart. Indeed, Gārgī, you have questioned about Brahman, and I have answered you about Brahman. Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among his own people.
Breath indeed is the eldest and the best;
he becomes the eldest and the best among his own people.
Moreover, he prospers with those for whom he desires to prosper—he who knows thus. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1)
*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 6.1.1*: "Om. It has been stated that 'the breath is the Gāyatrī.

For what reason, then, does the Gāyatrī have the nature of breath (*prāṇa*) and not the nature of speech and the other [senses]? Because the breath is both the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and the best (*śreṣṭha*), whereas speech and the others do not possess the qualities of being the eldest or the best. How is it that the breath possesses this quality of being the eldest and the best? With the desire to determine that, this [section] is commenced."

Alternatively, it has been stated that the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is to be performed by means of its states as the *ṛc*, *yajus*, *sāman*, the *kṣattra*, and so forth, even though other [organs] such as the eye exist.
In this context, the reason [for this] is connected immediately with what follows; it does not, however, constitute a mere continuation of the preceding section.
However, since this section (kāṇḍa) is supplementary (khila), that meditation concerning the vital breath (prāṇa) which possesses a specific fruit and was not mentioned previously must now be stated.

The particle "ha vai" is used for emphasis; whoever knows the one who possesses the qualities of being the oldest (jyeṣṭha) and the best (śreṣṭha), as will be described—that person indeed becomes both the oldest and the best.
Thus, being enticed by the prospect of the reward, he became ready to answer and said to him: "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the eldest and the best.
But how is it understood that the vital breath is the eldest and the best?
Because at the very moment of conception, the connection of the semen and the blood is common to the entire collection of factors beginning with the vital breath.
Nevertheless, since semen does not germinate if it is devoid of *prāṇa*, this is the first acquisition of function for *prāṇa* among the eyes and other senses;
therefore, *prāṇa* is the eldest in terms of age,
for from the time of conception, *prāṇa* nourishes the embryo.
For when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has first obtained its function, only then do the eyes and the other senses obtain their functions;
therefore, it is appropriate that the vital breath is the eldest among the eyes and so forth.
However, there may be someone who is the eldest in a family but, due to a lack of qualities, is not the best.

A middle son or a youngest son might become the best due to being rich in virtues, but not necessarily the eldest; however, it is not so in this case, for he says: "But the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is both the eldest and the best.
How, then, is the pre-eminence of the vital breath understood? We shall demonstrate that here through their dialogue.
In every way, however, he who knows and worships the vital breath (prāṇa) as possessing the qualities of being the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among his own kinsmen.

By the power of worshipping it as having the qualities of being the eldest and the best, even for those among whom he desires to be— the one wishing to become the eldest and the best— he who perceives the vital breath as the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among them as well.
And he becomes the most excellent.
[Objection: Is it not the case that seniority is based on age? How then can it be said to arise from his will?
[Response: This is not a fault.
Because it is intended to express that the "seniority" consists precisely in the attainment of its functional activity, like that of the vital breath (prāṇa). //1//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.2:
He who knows the most excellent becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech, indeed, is the most excellent.
He becomes the most excellent among his own people,
and also among those whom he wishes to excel—
provided he knows this. 6.1.2.
He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*) becomes the most excellent among his own people;
the fruit corresponds to the nature of that vision.
And he becomes the most excellent even for those among whom, apart from his kinsmen, he desires to be the most excellent.
Then let it be told: who is this Vasiṣṭha? Speech indeed is Vasiṣṭha;
she is called Vasiṣṭhā because she causes one to dwell (vāsayati) or because she clothes (vaste) exceedingly.
For eloquent speakers dwell exceedingly richly;
or [the word *vasiṣṭha*] is derived from the root *vas*,
meaning "to clothe," for eloquent speakers indeed surpass others in speech.
Thus, through the thorough knowledge of the qualities of Vasiṣṭha, one comes to possess the qualities of Vasiṣṭha; this is the fruit corresponding to the vision. //2//
He who knows the foundation indeed stands firm on even ground;
he stands firm on difficult ground.
The eye, indeed, is the foundation;
for by means of the eye one stands firm on both the level and the uneven ground.
One stands firm on the level; one stands firm on the uneven.
He who knows thus. BrhUp 6.1.3.

Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 6.1.3: "He who knows the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) truly becomes established by means of it"—this is the foundation. He who knows that foundation as possessing the quality of being a foundation, for him this is the fruit: he becomes established on level ground and at the proper time;
likewise, even in difficult terrain, on uneven ground, or in a place hard to traverse, or at a difficult time such as a famine.
If this is so, let it be told: what is that foundation?
The eye, indeed, is the foundation.
How is it that the eye possesses the nature of a foundation? He says: for by means of the eye, having seen both the level and the difficult terrain, one stands firm.
"Therefore, he who knows thus finds his footing in a corresponding fruit; he finds his footing on even ground and in difficult terrain. //3//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.4:
He who knows attainment—for him whatever desire he desires is indeed attained.
The ear, verily, is attainment.
For all these Vedas are fully contained within the ear.
Whatever desire he may desire, it is fulfilled for him who knows this. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.4)
"Whoever knows attainment—that is, whoever knows that which is endowed with the quality of attainment—for him this result is attained.
What is it? Whatever desire he desires, that desire [is fulfilled]."
What, then, is the quality of perfection? The ear is indeed perfection.
But how is it that the ear possesses the quality of perfection?

It is said: Since all the Vedas are fully realized when the ear exists—because they are to be studied by one who possesses the sense of hearing—and since desires depend upon the ritual acts prescribed in the Vedas, therefore the ear is prosperity.
Consequently, the fruit corresponds to the consciousness [of the agent].
Whatever desire he desires, it is fulfilled for him who knows thus. //4//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.5:
He who knows the abode becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men.
Mind, indeed, is the abode.
He who knows this becomes a place of refuge for his own people and a place of refuge for all men. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.5)
"He who knows the abode"—the abode is the support; he who knows that becomes the abode for his own people and the abode for other people as well. But what, then, is that abode?
It is said: the mind is indeed the basis and the support for both the sense-faculties and their objects;

for it is when dependent upon the mind that objects attain the status of being experienced by the self, and it is under the influence of the mind’s volitions that the sense-faculties proceed and cease.
Therefore, the mind-base (manas-āyatana) is the faculty of the senses.
Therefore, according to one's vision, the fruit becomes the base for oneself and the base for people; for one who knows thus. //5//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.6:
He who knows procreation (prajāti) is indeed procreated with offspring and cattle;
for semen is procreation.
He who knows thus is indeed procreated with offspring and cattle. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.6.
He who knows procreation (prajāti) is indeed procreated; he becomes endowed with offspring and cattle.
Semen is indeed procreation;
by means of semen, the generative organ is indicated.
Indeed, a fruit corresponding to that knowledge arises for one who knows this, [consisting] of offspring and cattle. //6//
These vital breaths (*prāṇas*), disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahman.
They said to him: "Which of us is the most excellent?"
He said to them: "Among you, when one has departed, that by whose departure this body is considered worse off—he among you is the most excellent."

These vital breaths— speech and the others— quarreling for the sake of "I am the better one," that is, for the purpose of establishing who was superior, went to Brahman; having gone to Prajāpati, who is denoted by the word "Brahman," they said this to him.
"Who among us is the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*)? Who among us dwells and causes [others] to dwell?

Thus questioned by them, that Brahman spoke as follows: "When, among you, whichever one has departed—that is, has gone out from the body—the world considers this body to be more wretched (*pāpīyaḥ*), that is, more evil than it was before."
For this body, because it is a collection of many impurities, is indeed evil even while alive; it is even more wretched when [the soul] has departed from it.
This is stated—"it is most evil"—for the purpose of generating detachment.
Among you, he shall be the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*). Although Prajāpati knew who Vasiṣṭha was, he said, "This one is Vasiṣṭha," in order to avoid displeasing the others. (7)
Speech went out.
Having been away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?"
They said: "Just as we lived—speaking with speech, breathing with breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so did we live.
Then Speech entered back into him. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.1.8.

Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, those vital breaths (prāṇas) departed from the body one after another in order to test their own strength. There, speech itself was the first to depart from this body;
having departed and stayed away for a year—that is, having remained absent—it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me? How did you have the power to exist apart from me?"
Thus addressed, they replied: "Just as in the world those who are unskilled and mute live—performing the activity of breathing with the breath (*prāṇa*) though not speaking with speech;

performing the activity of seeing with the eye though not seeing; hearing with the ear; knowing with the mind regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done; and procreating sons with semen—so indeed have we lived. Thus they spoke.
Having understood that speech had remained behind in this body while the vital breaths had departed, speech indeed entered back into it.
Then the eye departed.
After staying away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?"

They said: "Just as those who are blind live without seeing with the eye, yet breathe with the breath, speak with speech, hear with the ear, know with the mind, and procreate with semen—even so have we lived.
Thereupon, the eye entered [the body]. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.1.9.
The ear departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?

They replied, "Just as those who are deaf live—without hearing with the ear, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so did we live."
It entered the ear. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.10.
The mind departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?
They replied: "Just as ignorant, simple-minded people live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and procreating with semen—even so did we live."
The mind entered. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.11.
The semen departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "Just as eunuchs live without procreating, breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind—thus have we lived."
It entered as semen. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.12.
Likewise, "The eye indeed departed," and so forth, as before;
[the others are] the ear, the mind, and procreation. //9–12//
Then,
as the vital breath was about to depart, it tore up these other breaths just as a great, well-bred Sindhava horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers;
they said, "O Venerable One, do not depart!"
"We shall certainly not be able to live without you.
"Then bring tribute to me," he said.
"So be it," they replied. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.13)

Now, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was about to depart—that is, about to perform its departure—speech and the other organs immediately began to stir from their own places. To illustrate this, he says: "Just as in the world, a great and fine horse—a *mahāsuhaya*, meaning a beautiful horse endowed with auspicious marks, large in size, a *saindhava* born in the Sindhu region by lineage—[stirs] the pegs of the foot-tethers; and these *paḍvīśas* are the pegs for binding the feet."
The horseman, for the sake of testing him while he was mounted, should simultaneously pull up those pegs, lift them, and dig them out all at once;
in this very way, he [Death] pulled out these vital breaths, speech and the rest, having restrained them and caused them to fall from their respective places.
Then those [breaths], speech and the others, said: "O Venerable One, do not depart, for indeed we shall not be able to live without you."
"If you have thus recognized my superiority—if I am the best among you here—then pay tribute to me, offer me a tax.
This dialogue regarding the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is an instruction on the method for examining who is superior among the wise;
for by this means, a wise person examines [the matter], thinking, "Who indeed is the best here?"
This method of examination is stated as being consistent with the context;
for otherwise, it would not be possible for these [organs], acting in concert, to depart one by one in such a straightforward manner over the course of exactly one year.
Therefore, it is only the wise man who, desiring to know the principal among speech and the other organs for the sake of meditation, investigates them in this manner.
Being thus requested by Bali, the vital breaths promised, saying, "So be it. //13//
Then Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent;
insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation," [said] the Eye.
Or, "Whatever perfection I am, you are that perfection"—this is the ear.
Or, "Whatever abode I am, you are that abode"—this is the mind.
Or, "Whatever procreation I am, you are that procreation"—this is semen.
"What is my food? What is my clothing? [He replied: "Whatever there is here, down to dogs, down to worms, down to insects and moths—that is your food. Water is your clothing."
Verily, no food that is unfit for eating is consumed by him, nor is any such food accepted, who knows this food of the breath (*anasya annam*) in this way.
Knowing this, learned Vedic scholars sip water before eating and sip water after eating;
they do so thinking that they are thereby making this very food non-naked (*anagnam*).

That Speech, indeed, being the first to proceed to offer tribute, spoke as follows: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*), whatever excellence belongs to me is yours alone; by that quality of being most excellent, you are that most excellent one.
Or: "Insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation; whatever foundation is mine, that you are."
The eye;
the rest is the same.
They have successively presented [the topics of] the sense-bases, birth, the skin, and the qualities.
"If it is so, you have indeed given an excellent offering; tell me, what is the food and what is the clothing for him who is distinguished by such qualities?

They replied: "Whatever is called food in this world, from dogs down to worms and down to insects and moths—whatever is the food of dogs, the food of worms, and the food of insects and moths, along with all that whatsoever is being eaten by living beings—all that is your food; everything is the food of Prāṇa."
In this context, a specific view is being prescribed.
Some, who are experts in the science of vital breaths (*prāṇānnavid*), claim that there is no fault in eating all things;
that is incorrect.
If it is argued that this [position] is a conceptual construction because it is prohibited by another scripture,
we say no;
for that [scripture] is not prescriptive.
"Indeed, nothing that is not food is ever eaten by him"—this is for the purpose of praising the enjoined knowledge that "everything is food for the vital breath" (prāṇa).

This is because it forms a single syntactical unit with that injunction. It does not, however, have the power to sublate what is enjoined in other scriptures, since this statement is intended for another purpose.
The intended teaching here is the vision that "all food belongs to the vital breath alone" (prāṇamātra), and not the injunction "one should eat everything.
As for the notion that there is no fault in eating all things, that is merely false, as it lacks any authoritative basis.
If it is argued that because the knower is essentially the vital breath, the consumption of all food is logically consistent and thus by implication free from fault, we say: no.
Because it is impossible for [the wise one] to eat all food without exception.

True; even though the wise one is the vital breath (prāṇa), by means of that aggregate of body and organs with which he is qualified as a "wise one," it is not possible for him to consume all food—such as worms, insects, gods, and so forth—by means of that very aggregate of body and organs.
Therefore, in that case, the purpose of making known the absence of fault in eating all food would be meaningless.
Because the fault of eating all food without exception has not been incurred.
But surely, being the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it does indeed consume even the food of worms, insects, and so forth? Certainly.
However, there is no prohibition regarding that [color].
Therefore, since the *kiṃśuka* flower is naturally red, there is an absence of fault in that case;
thus, it is useless to indicate the absence of fault by means of its specific form.

Because the fault of eating all food without remainder has not been incurred, there is no counter-exception (pratiprasava) here with respect to that connection to the aggregate of body and organs by which the prohibition was originally made. Therefore, if one transgresses that prohibition, there will indeed be a fault; for the passage beginning with "na ha vā" refers to a different subject matter.

Nor is it taught here that the body of a Brāhmaṇa or others is to be seen as the food for all; rather, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone that is intended. And just as the vital breath, which generally consumes all food, has certain types of food as the cause of its sustenance for this or that being—for instance, poison is the very food of a poison-born insect, yet even that same poison, when seen by another, produces a defect characterized by death and so forth—so it is here.
Likewise, even for one whose life-force (*prāṇa*) consists of all food, there would indeed be a fault in eating forbidden food due to the connection with a body such as that of a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the notion that there is no fault in eating what should not be eaten is merely false knowledge.
[In the passage] "Water is your garment," water being consumed stands in the place of a garment for you.
And here, the instruction "water is the garment of the vital breath" (prāṇa) is enjoined as a meditative vision;
however, water cannot be employed for the actual function of a garment.
Therefore, one should perform this merely as a meditative vision while continuing the consumption of water as it naturally occurs.
"Verily, for one who knows this, there is no such thing as non-food; that is to say, nothing whatsoever that is not food—that which is unfit to be eaten—becomes eaten or consumed by him.

Even if he has consumed something unfit to be eaten, it becomes as if only fit food were consumed; he is not tainted by the defect resulting from that act. We have already stated that this is a praise of the knowledge [of the Self]. Likewise, there is no such thing as a gift that is not food; even if he should receive something unfit to be accepted, such as an elephant or the like, that too becomes food."
Even in that case, one would not be tainted by the fault of accepting what is not to be accepted; this is merely for the sake of praise:

"He who thus knows this food of the breath, the breath. As for the fruit, it is indeed the state of being the self of the breath, but not with the intention of [promising] that specific fruit; rather, it is with the intention of praise.
But why does this very thing not constitute the fruit?
It is not the case that for one who perceives the vital breath as the Self, the mere state of being the vital breath is the fruit;
rather, for one who has become the vital breath—the Self of all—even that which is inedible must indeed be eaten.
Thus, even that which is not to be accepted is indeed to be accepted; knowledge is praised by taking up exactly what is obtained.
Therefore, this sentence does not have the form of an injunction regarding a result.

Because water is the garment of the vital breath (prāṇa), therefore learned Brāhmaṇas—those who are *śrotriya* and have studied the Vedas—sip water before eating (*aśiṣyantaḥ*), meaning they sip water when about to eat; and having eaten, they sip water afterwards.
They eat it.
Regarding this, what is the intention behind their rinsing the mouth? He says: they think that by doing so, they are making this very vital breath (prāṇa) unclothed.
And this is indeed the case; for when someone gives a garment to another, he thinks, "I am making him unclothed."
For it has been stated that "water is the garment of the vital breath.
This is intended for the purpose of cultivating the realization: "When I drink water, I am giving a garment to the vital breath.
Now, one might object: "One sips water both before eating and after eating with the thought, 'I shall become pure.'"
Furthermore, if the purpose [of the sipping] were to ensure that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not "naked," then the act of sipping would have two distinct effects;
yet it is not logical for a single act of sipping to have two effects.

If it is for the sake of purification (*prāyatya*), it is not for the sake of making [the breath] non-naked; and if it is for the sake of making [the breath] non-naked, it is not for the sake of purification.

Since this is so, [the opponent argues: "Therefore, let there be a second sipping of water (ācamana) subsequent to the first, for the purpose of making the vital breath (prāṇa) 'unclothed' (anagnatā). [The author replies:
No, because two distinct actions are logically established.
For these two actions—the sipping of water prescribed by Smṛti for one who is about to eat and for one who has already eaten—are for the purpose of purification (prāyatya).

It is merely an action, and it does not require purification (*prāyatya*) or depend upon seeing [the water] and so forth. Furthermore, in that context, the perception of the garment within the water—which serves as a subsidiary part of the sipping (*ācamana*)—is enjoined as a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) for the vital breath (*prāṇa*); however, when that [perception] is performed, the fact that the sipping has the purpose of purification is not sublated, because the sipping remains a distinct action.
Therefore, this applies to the sipping performed by one who is about to eat or has already eaten.
The statement "Water is indeed the garment of breath" is enjoined as a mere meditative visualization (darśana), because it is not established by any other means. //14//
Thus ends the first Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.1:
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya came to the assembly of the Pañcālas.
He approached Jaivali Pravāhaṇa while he was being waited upon.
Looking at him, he said, "O boy! He replied, "Yes, sir! [The father asked: "Have you been instructed by your father?"
"Om," he said. Brhadaranyaka Upanishad 6.2.1.
Regarding the passage beginning "Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi": this is the connection.
This is a supplementary section (*khila-adhikāra*) wherein that which was not previously stated is now being declared.
At the end of the seventh chapter, one who practices the combination of knowledge and action made a request for the path from Agni, saying: "O Agni, lead us by a good path."

In this context, the existence of many paths is demonstrated by the power of the mantra through the qualification "good path" (*supatha*). Furthermore, "paths" refers to the paths of practice for the realization of the ripening of karma.
And he will say, "Having done what," and so forth.
In that context, this undertaking is for the purpose of summarizing all the destinies of saṃsāra, as to how many paths there are for the realization of the maturation of karma;
for such is the extent of the destinies of saṃsāra.
Such is the ripening of action— both that which is innate and that which is scriptural— along with consciousness.
Although the innate evil was indicated in the passage, "Two [beings] indeed were born of Prajāpati," its effect as a ripening was not demonstrated there.
However, the ripening (*vipāka*) of that which is indeed scriptural has been demonstrated up to the realization of the threefold self (*tryannātman*),
because detachment from that is intended at the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Even there, it was stated that the world of the fathers is attained through mere ritual action (*karman*), while the world of the gods is attained through knowledge (*vidyā*) and through action conjoined with knowledge.

In that regard, it has not been stated by which path one reaches the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) or by which the world of the gods (devaloka). Since this must be explained in its entirety here in this section on the "Remaining Topics" (khilaprakaraṇa), it is now commenced; for a summary of everything at the end is desired in a treatise.

Moreover, although it has been stated that "immortality is only this much" and that "there is no hope for immortality through ritual action," the reason for that was not explicitly stated; it is for that purpose that this [section] begins.

Since this is the destination of ritual action and there is no operation toward eternal immortality, it follows by implication that "only this much" constitutes the means to immortality, thereby establishing its status as the reason.

Furthermore, it was said regarding the Agnihotra: "But you do not know their departure, nor their path, nor their support, nor their satisfaction, nor their return, nor the world that rises up to meet them."

In that response, beginning with the words "these two oblations, when offered, depart," the effect of the oblation has been stated. And this is the fruit of the action characterized as the oblation performed by an agent;
for it is not possible for an action characterized as an oblation to initiate an effect such as departure independently, without depending upon an agent.
Because the action is for the sake of the agent,
and because the action depends upon the means of accomplishment,
it has been stated that the "task" (kārya) belongs to the Agnihotra alone in all six ways, since it serves the purpose of praising the Agnihotra.
But here, it is taught that the fruit belongs to the agent alone,
because the knowledge of the sixfold fruit of action is intended to be explained.
And by means of that, the vision of the five fires is intended to be prescribed here as the means for attaining the northern path.

Thus, having shown the inclusion of all the courses of transmigratory existence, and wishing to demonstrate these two points—that this is the final conclusion of the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa)—the author introduces a narrative.
Śvetaketu by name was the son of Āruṇi; Āruṇi was the son of Aruṇa, and his son was Āruṇeya.
The word *ha* signifies tradition;
*vai* signifies certainty.

Having been instructed by his father, he came to the assembly of the Pañcālas for the sake of proclaiming his own fame; out of pride, thinking "having conquered [them], I shall also conquer the assembly of the king," he arrived there.
The son of Jīvala was the King of Pañcāla named Pravāhaṇa, who was being attended by his own servants and was causing them to attend upon himself—that is, making them perform service for him.

That king, having previously heard of the pride arising from that man's conceit regarding his learning and thinking, "This man must be disciplined," looked up at him as he approached; and as soon as he had arrived, he addressed him, calling out "Kumāra!"—the protracted vowel (*pluti*) being used for the purpose of rebuking him.
Being thus addressed, he replied, "Bho!
Being angry, he had answered the Kṣatriya with "Bho! even though it was an improper form of address.
The king said, "Have you been instructed? Have you been taught by your father? Thus he spoke.
The other replied, "Om, yes; I have been instructed. Ask, if you have any doubt. (1)
"Do you know how these creatures, when departing, diverge?
"No," he said.
"Do you know how they return again to this world?
"No," he replied.
"Do you know how that world is not filled up, even though many people go there again and again?"
"No," he replied.
"Do you know on which oblation being offered the waters, having assumed human voices, rise up and speak?
"No," he replied.
Do you know the starting point of the path leading to the gods, or of the path leading to the ancestors—
that which, having performed, people set out upon the path to the gods or the path to the ancestors?
For indeed, we have heard the word of the seer:
"I have heard of two paths for the fathers—those of the gods and those of mortals.
Along these two, all this moving world comes together, that which lies between the father and the mother.
"I do not know even one of them," he said. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.2)
If you know thus—do you understand in what manner, by what means, these well-known creatures, when they die and depart (*prayatyaḥ*), "fall apart" (*vipratipadyante*)?

The protracted vowel (*pluti*) is for the sake of deliberation. It refers to the divergence of paths for those traveling along a common way, wherein some creatures go by one path and others by another; this is the "falling apart."
The meaning is: "Do you know how those creatures go astray?
The other replied, "No.
"Then do you know how they return to this world—that is, how they come back to this world again?"
"No," Śvetaketu replied.
"Do you know how it is that this world is not filled up— by what process it is that this world is not filled up again and again by those who die and go there?"
"No," he said,
"do you know on which [numbered] oblation— on the offering of how many oblations— the waters, having become 'human-voiced' (puruṣavācaḥ)— that is, having acquired speech identical to that of a human,
or being designated by the word 'human'— [arise]?"
"When they have transformed into the form of men, then they possess human speech;
having arisen, having properly arisen, being born, they speak as beings.
"No," he said.
"Then, transformed into the form of a man, they come to have the speech of a man; having arisen, having arisen rightly, being born, they speak. "No," he replied.

If you know thus the point of departure—that is, the means by which one sets out—of the path leading to the gods (*devayāna*), or the point of departure of the path leading to the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*; the meaning expressed by the word "point of departure" is this): namely, having performed what kind of action—meaning, having performed a specific action—one sets out upon the path leading to the gods or the path leading to the fathers. It refers to that action by performing which they set out.
That action is called "the way" (pratipad); the meaning is: "Do you know that way, or do you know the means for attaining the world of the gods and the world of the ancestors?
Furthermore, we have heard a statement from a seer's mantra that illuminates this very matter.
The meaning is that there also exists a mantra which illuminates this very point.
What is that mantra? It is said:
"I have heard of two paths, two ways; of these, one leads to the ancestors, being connected with the world of the fathers; by that path, one reaches the world of the fathers. This is the meaning.
The phrase "I have heard" is to be connected with what follows.
Furthermore, there is another path belonging to the gods which leads to the gods.
But who, by means of these two paths, goes to both the ancestors and the gods?
It is said: "Furthermore, belonging to mortals—that is, to human beings—for it is humans alone who go by means of the two paths;
the meaning is that by those two paths this entire universe goes, comes together, and meets.
And those two paths are between—meaning within the interval of—the father and the mother, that is, in the middle between mother and father."
The two parents are the two halves of the cosmic egg, heaven and earth;
for it has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa: "This is indeed the mother, that is the father.
Between these two halves of the egg, within the sphere of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), lie these two paths, not for the sake of attaining absolute immortality.
The other said: "Of this entire collection of questions, I do not know even a single one; I do not know," Śvetaketu replied. //2//
Then he invited him to stay for the night;
disregarding the invitation to stay, the boy ran away.
He went to his father, who said to him:
"Is it true, as I have heard, that you previously told us we had been instructed?
How so, Sumedha?"
"A kinsman of royalty asked me five questions; of those, I did not know even one. Which were they? he said.
"These," he said, "are the introductory formulas. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.3)

Then, immediately after removing the pride of his conceit regarding his learning, the king invited the aforementioned Śvetaketu for the purpose of providing him lodging, saying, "May you dwell here; let water for the feet and the guest-offering be brought. Disregarding that invitation to stay, the youth Śvetaketu ran away back toward his father.
He went to his father and said to him, "How is it, indeed, that you previously spoke to us regarding our father in such a manner?

He went to his father and said to him, "How is it, indeed, that you previously, at the time of our return [from study], spoke to us—having instructed us with all branches of knowledge—in such a manner? Having heard these reproachful words of his son, the father said:

"In what manner, O wise one—*sumedhas*, meaning one whose intelligence (*medhā*) is excellent—has this suffering arisen for you? Listen to how it happened from me. [Answer] my five questions, that is, those numbering five. [The king says: 'O kinsman of royalty' (*rājanyabandhu*). This term 'kinsman of royalty' is a word of contempt."
He then asked him; [the son replied] that he did not know—not even one—of those questions.
When his father asked, "Which were the questions asked by the kings?", the son cited the introductory phrases—the openings—of those questions, saying, "These are they. //3//
He said: "My dear, you should know us thus: whatever I know, all that I have told you. But go now there."
"Let us both live the holy life together.
"May you go yourself," he replied.
Then Gautama went to where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was.

Therefore, having brought a seat, he caused water to be brought. Then he offered him the *arghya* (water of honor). He said to him: "We grant a boon to the venerable Gautama. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.4)

The father, pacifying his angry son, said: "In that manner, my dear child, you should understand and accept us such that you know: 'Whatever collection of knowledge I know, all of that I have told you.
Who else is more beloved to me than you, for whose sake I would have guarded [this knowledge]?"
"I too do not know what the king has asked. Therefore, go; come back here, and having gone there, we two shall live the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of knowledge.
He said, "May you yourself go; I do not venture to look upon his face."

Gautama of the Gautama lineage, the son of Aruṇi, arrived at the place where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali had prepared a seat—a formal reception with two sets of six cushions—for his arrival. When Gautama had arrived, he had a suitable seat brought for him and had water served by his attendants. Then, through his domestic priest, he offered him the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) accompanied by sacred mantras.
Having performed this worship, he said to him, "I shall grant a boon to you, the venerable Gautama," referring to [the gift] characterized by cows, horses, and so forth. //4//
He said: "This boon has been promised to me.
But as for that word which you spoke in the presence of the boy, tell that to me."

Gautama said: "This boon was promised by you to me; in order to make yourself firm in this promise, tell me that very speech which you uttered in the presence of my son—that speech in the form of a question—for that alone shall be our boon."
He said: "Gautama, those [boons] are indeed among the divine;
speak for the human ones."
The king said: "O Gautama, regarding those boons among the gods, that which you seek is indeed one of the human boons; choose another boon."
He said: "It is well known that I have acquired much gold, elephants, cattle, horses, female slaves, attendants, and clothing.
May you not, sir, be one who diminishes this great, infinite, and boundless wealth of ours."
"O Gautama, you may seek [instruction] through the proper way. "I shall approach you as a pupil," he said.
Formerly, they used to enter [as pupils] by word alone.
He lived there, making his arrival known.
Gautama said: "That [knowledge] is indeed known to you as well; I have it.
I have no need for that human boon which you wish to give me.

For I already possess abundant gold, I have obtained cattle and horses—I have obtained them—and this phrase applies to all [the following]: female slaves, excellent attendants, retinues, and clothing."
Furthermore, that which exists for me in reality is neither to be requested by you nor to be given by you; moreover,
you yourself know that the boon was promised by you and that it is proper here for you to preserve your promise.

Furthermore, my intention is this: let it not be that you, having been generous toward us alone, should become ungenerous toward others; that is to say, let him not be stingy. "Of much" means abundant; "of infinite" means of infinite fruit.
"Of boundless" means inexhaustible; that is to say, [fruit] which extends to one's sons, grandsons, and so forth.
"May you not be the one who takes away such wealth from me alone;
there is nothing else that ought not to be given by you.

Being addressed thus, he said: "O Gautama, you indeed desire to obtain knowledge from me through the proper ford, that is, by the right method prescribed in the scriptures. Thus addressed, Gautama said: "I approach you; I come to you as a disciple."
Regarding the word "bhavantam" (you):

it is said that in former times, Brāhmaṇas seeking knowledge would indeed approach Kṣatriyas, or Kṣatriyas would approach Vaiśyas, or Vaiśyas [would approach others] in times of distress; for they approached them in the manner of disciples, and not with the formal rites of approaching a teacher (*upāyana*) or service (*śuśrūṣā*), and so forth.
Therefore...
That Gautama, by the mere mention of the name of the gift—simply by the renown of coming with a gift—stayed there as a guest, but did not actually present the gift. //7//
He said: "In this way, O Gautama, neither you nor your ancestors have committed an offense against us,
since this knowledge has never before dwelt with any Brahmin."
"I shall indeed tell it to you;
for who would refuse one who speaks thus? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.8)
When Gautama had thus spoken in the midst of the assembly, the king, perceiving him to be distressed, said this while seeking his forgiveness: "May you not commit an offense against us;

that is to say, our offense should not be taken to heart. Furthermore, just as your ancestors did not accept any offense from our ancestors, so too should you maintain the conduct of your ancestors toward us."

"Just as this knowledge has been sought by you, and prior to its transmission to you, it never resided with any Brāhmaṇa—since you yourself know that this knowledge has always come down through the lineage of Kṣatriyas—that tradition must be preserved by me as well, if it is possible," he said. To which [Gautama] replied: "O Gautama, among the boons granted by the gods, speak for humans; however, this is not to be given to you."
"Very well," [he said]. "From now on, it is no longer possible to protect it.
Nevertheless, I shall impart that very knowledge to you; for who else indeed would be able to refuse you when you speak thus, saying 'I will not tell you'? "How then could I not tell it to you? (8)
"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire;
the sun is its fuel."
The rays are the smoke;
the day is the flame;
the quarters are the embers.
The intermediate directions are the sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation.
From that oblation, King Soma comes into being.

The fourth question—"That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire"—is settled first. This reversal of the order [of questions] is for the sake of settling this one, since the settlement of the other questions depends upon it.

That celestial world, O Gautama, is the fire; the perception of fire is enjoined with respect to the celestial world, which is not itself fire, just as [the perception of fire is enjoined] with respect to a woman or a man. Of that celestial-world-fire, the sun alone is the fuel, because it kindles it.
For that world is kindled by the sun;
its smoke is the rays, because of their commonality in rising,
for the rays have issued forth from the sun.
The fuel is smoke, for it rises into the world; the flame is the day, due to the commonality of luminosity;
the embers are the quarters of space, due to the commonality of subsiding.
The intermediate directions are the sparks, because they are scattered like sparks.

Into this very fire of the heavenly world, characterized by such qualities, the gods—Indra and the others—offer faith as the substance of the oblation; they cast it in. From that offering, King Soma comes into being for the ancestors and for the Brahmins.

Regarding this, [the question arises: who are the deities there, how do they offer, and what is the oblation called "faith"? We have already explained this in the *Saṃbandha* (Introduction). However, for the purpose of determining the meaning of the six categories beginning with "But you certainly do not perceive their departure," it was explained in the context of the *Agnihotra*:
"When these two *Agnihotra* oblations have been offered, they depart."
They enter the intermediate space;
they make the intermediate space the Āhavanīya fire, the wind the fuel, and the rays the bright oblation.
They satisfy the intermediate space.
They ascend from there;
they enter heaven;
they make heaven the Āhavanīya fire and the sun the fuel—thus it has been stated.
In that regard, the two *agnihotra* oblations depart together with their constituent means.

Just as here they are known to be distinguished by specific means—namely, the *āhavanīya* fire, fuel, smoke, embers, sparks, and the substance of the oblation—in that same manner they depart from this world to that world.
There, the fire remains as fire, the fuel as fuel, the smoke as smoke, the embers as embers, the sparks as sparks, and the substance of the oblation likewise.
Milk and other substances intended as offering-materials for the *āhuti* exist even in the undifferentiated state at the beginning of creation, persisting in a subtle form through the Supreme Self.

That very Agnihotra rite, together with its constituent means, existing in the form of the *apūrva*, remains established; then, at the time of differentiation, it undergoes transformation by assuming the state of the intermediate space and so forth, and the *āhavanīya* fire and other such elements.

In the same way, even now there is the ritual known as the Agnihotra. Thus, the entire world consists of the transformation of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) resulting from the Agnihotra oblations. For the purpose of praising these two oblations alone, the six topics beginning with "departing" and ending with "rising up toward the world" have been determined below in the section on ritual action (*karmaprakaraṇa*).

In this context, however, since the agent’s own actions are intended to be described, the vision of the five fires—beginning with the heavenly world and Agni—is introduced as a means for attaining the northern path (*uttaramārga*) for the sake of experiencing the fruits of specific karma.
Thus, the vision of the heavenly world, Agni, and so forth is set forth.

In that regard, those very vital breaths (*prāṇas*) which are internal here as the offerers (*hotṛ*) of the Agnihotra become Indra and the other deities when transformed into their external, divine form; these same beings are the offerers there in the fire of the heavenly world.

And they, having performed the *agnihotra* here for the sake of enjoying its fruit, indeed attain the state of being offerers (*hotṛ*) in various places even at the time when that fruit is ripening, because they are the enjoyers of that fruit as it transforms accordingly; thus, undergoing such transformations, they come to be designated by the term "gods" (*deva*).

And in this regard, the substance of milk which served as the basis for the *agnihotra* rite, having been cast here into the *āhavanīya* fire and consumed by the fire, [is transformed] by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Transformed into a subtle form, together with the agent—the sacrificer—it enters that world, the heavenly realm from the intermediate space, by way of smoke and so forth.

Those subtle waters, which have become the effect of the oblation, are inherent in the *agnihotra*, and accompanied by the agent, are denoted by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*). As they enter the heavenly world to initiate another body for the agent in the world of Soma, they are said to be "offered."
Having entered the heavenly world there, they initiate the body of the agent within the lunar orb.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The gods offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation, King Soma arises.
For the scripture declares: "Faith, indeed, is the waters."
The question—"Do you know in which oblation, when offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak?"—and its resolution—"That world, indeed, is the fire"—have been introduced.
From this, it is determined that the waters, which are inherent in ritual action, initiate the body of the agent, and are denoted by the term *śraddhā*.
Because of their predominance, they are designated as "human speech," but this does not mean that the other elements are absent.
The initiation of the body is impelled by karma,
and karma is inherent in water;
therefore, water holds primacy in the act of creating the body.
And by that [process], there is the designation "the waters have the voice of a person.
For everywhere, the commencement of birth is caused by karma.

In this regard, although the six topics beginning with departure (utkrānti) were introduced in connection with the Agnihotra through the medium of praising the Agnihotra oblation, nevertheless, all Vedic rituals beginning with the Agnihotra are included.
They are indicated [in the scriptures].
For, having introduced the fivefold ritual connected with wife and fire, it is said: "By action, the world of the fathers.
And the author will say later: "Now, those who win the worlds by sacrifice, by charity, and by austerity. (9)
"Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed Agni;
the year is his fuel."
The clouds are its smoke;
lightning is its flame;
and thunderbolts are its embers.
The thunderclaps are the sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as an oblation;
from that offering, rain comes into being.
"Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the second fire—the substratum for the oblation—according to the sequence of the two oblations' return.
Parjanya is the name of the divine self who presides over the instruments of rain.
For him, the year itself is the fuel."
For the rain-cloud, which is Agni, blazes forth by means of its own constituent parts— the year revolving through the seasons beginning with autumn and ending with summer;
the clouds are its smoke,
because they originate from smoke or because they are perceived as being like smoke.
Lightning is its flame,
due to the commonality of luminosity;
thunderbolts are its embers.
[The clouds] are characterized by the common qualities of tranquility and solidity. The *hrādunayaḥ* and *hlādunayaḥ* are the sounds of thunder, which are the sparks [of lightning].
This is due to the commonality of their dispersion and multiplicity.
In this very context, there is a specification of the locus for the constant oblation:
"The gods"—meaning those same priests—offer King Soma.
That Soma which was produced when the oblation of faith was poured into the fire of the heavenly world is offered into the second fire, that of Parjanya.
And from that oblation of Soma, rain comes into being. //10//
"This world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama;
its fuel is the earth."
Fire is the smoke;
night is the flame;
the moon is the embers.
The stars are the sparks.
Into this very fire the gods offer rain;
from that offering, food comes into being.
"This world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire.
This world—the locus for the experience of living beings' births, characterized by actions, agents, and their fruits—is the third fire.
Of that fire, the earth itself is the fuel.
For this world is kindled by the earth, which is endowed with the enjoyment of manifold living beings;
smoke is fire,
due to the commonality of arising from a support, namely the earth.
For fire arises depending upon fuel that is of an earthly nature,
just as smoke arises depending upon kindling,
and its radiance depends upon the night.

This is due to the commonality of arising from a connection with fuel (*samit*). For indeed, through its connection with fuel, a flame arises from fire; likewise, through its connection with the earth as fuel, the night arises.
For they call that which is the shadow of the earth "śārvara";
the moon is the embers,
because of the commonality of being produced from that.
For just as embers arise from flames, so does the moon appear at night;
or because of their commonality in being subsided,
the stars are like sparks.
Because the scattering [of the elements] is similar to sparks.
"In that very one," and so forth, as before.
They offer rain as an oblation; from that oblation, food comes into being.
Because it is well known that food such as rice and barley originates from rain. //11//
"Man indeed is the fire, O Gautama;
his opened mouth is the fuel."
The vital breath is the smoke;
speech is the flame;
the eye is the embers.
The ear is the sparks.
Into this very fire the gods offer food;
from that offering, semen comes into being.
The person (*puruṣa*), O Gautama, is indeed the fire; this is well known. The person, possessing a head, hands, and so forth, is the fourth fire. His open mouth is the fuel (*samit*).

For by means of his open mouth, the person shines while speaking, reciting the Vedas, and so on, just as a fire shines by means of fuel. Breath (*prāṇa*) is the smoke, because of the similarity in their rising upward.
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arises from the mouth;
the word "speech" (*vākya*) is used for "light" (*arcis*) because of the common quality of being a manifestor,
and light is indeed a manifestor.
Likewise, the word "speech" (vāk) is the manifestor of that which is to be expressed;
the "embers" (aṅgāra) are the eyes, either because of the commonality of tranquility or because of being the locus of light;
the "sparks" (visphuliṅga) are the ears, due to the commonality of distraction.
In that [fire], they offer food.
Now, one might object: "Are not the gods ever seen here offering food?
This is no fault.
Because the vital breaths (prāṇas) possess the nature of deities:

the deities such as Indra and others in the sphere of the divine (adhidaiva) are themselves the vital breaths in the sphere of the self (adhyātma), and they are the ones who cast the food into the person.
From that oblation, semen comes into being.
For semen is indeed the transformation of food. //12//
A woman, indeed, is fire, O Gautama; her lap is the fuel.
The body hairs are the smoke; the womb is the flame;
what one does within is the embers.
The sparks are the Abhinandas.
Into this very fire, the gods offer semen as an oblation;
from that oblation, a person comes into being.
He lives as long as he lives; then, when he dies— Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.13.
"A woman, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama.
"Woman" refers to a female; she is the fifth fire as the locus for the oblation. Her lap is the fuel, for by means of it she is kindled.
The body hairs are smoke, because of the commonality of their arising from that [fire]. The womb is the flame, because of the commonality of its color.
That which one does within is the embers; the internal activity of sexual intercourse is the embers, because of the commonality of being the cause for the subsiding of virility.

Sexual intercourse is the cause for the subsiding of vigor and other [virtues], just as the state of charcoal is the cause for the subsiding of fire. The delights are mere fragments of pleasure; because they share the quality of being trivial, they are like sparks.
Into that they offer semen;
from that oblation, a person comes into being.

Thus, being offered in succession into the fires of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman, and attaining a gradual increase in grossness by way of the states of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen, those things denoted by the word "faith" [attain this form].
The waters take on the word "person.
As for the fourth question—"Do you know at which oblation, when offered, the waters, having become human speech, arise and speak?"—that has now been resolved:
at the fifth oblation, when offered into the fire of the woman, the waters, having become semen, become human speech.

That person, having been born in this manner, lives for a certain period of time. It is said: as long as he lives—that is to say, for as long as there exists karma that serves as the cause for the persistence of this body.
Then, upon its exhaustion, at whatever time one dies. //13//
Then they carry him to the fire;
for him, the fire itself becomes the fire.
Peace, peace! Smoke, smoke! Flame, flame!
"Embers, embers!
Sparks, sparks!"—
in this very fire, the gods offer the person as a libation.
From that oblation, a person of radiant complexion comes into being.

Now, when he has died, the officiating priests carry him for Agni—that is, for the sake of the final oblation. For him who has become an oblation, the well-known fire itself is the locus of the offering; no other fire need be imagined.
The fuel, the kindling, the smoke, the flame, the embers, and the sparks are all exactly as they are well known in common experience; this is the meaning.

Into that [fire], they offer the man as the final oblation; from that oblation, a man of radiant complexion, exceedingly brilliant, comes into being—that is, he is produced—because he has been consecrated by the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the final oblation.
Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, venerate truth with faith— they pass into the light;
from the light, into the day.
From the day [he goes] to the waxing fortnight;
from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward;
from the months to the world of the gods.
From the world of the gods [they go] to the sun;
from the sun to lightning. A person consisting of mind, having approached those who are of lightning, leads them to the worlds of Brahman.
In those worlds of Brahman, they dwell as supreme beings in the highest distances;
for them there is no returning again.
Now, for the purpose of resolving the first question, [the text] says: "They. Who are they?
They are those who know this aforementioned vision of the five fires (*pañcāgnidarśana*).

By the word "thus" (*evam*), the five fires—distinguished by fire, fuel, smoke, flame, embers, sparks, faith, and so forth—as previously specified, are indicated; the meaning is that they know these very five fires in this manner.
But surely this vision has as its object only the observation of the Agnihotra oblation;
for it was stated there, in the determination of the six categories beginning with departure (*utkrānti*), that "they make heaven itself the Āhavanīya fire," and so forth.
Here too, there is much similarity, such as the world over there being the fire and the sun being the fuel, and so on.
Therefore, this view is merely a subordinate part of that [preceding discussion].

No; for it is appropriate to refer by means of the word "thus" (*evam*) only so far as the question and answer regarding "on which day" (*yatithyām*) are taken up. Since the question "on which day? and its corresponding answer are fully embraced, it is proper to refer to them with the word "thus."
Otherwise, the question would be purposeless, and since the number is already known, it would be the fires themselves that ought to be mentioned.
If, on the other hand, what is already known is being restated,
then it is proper to restate only what has been established [by scripture], and not that "this world is the fire."
Now, even if it were intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would still be more appropriate to illustrate by means of both the first and the last [terms],
and because of another scriptural passage (*śruti*).

For in the *Chāndogya* scripture, within the same context, it says "one knows the five fires," and since only the number five is mentioned there, this [passage] is not a supplement to the *agnihotra*.
Regarding the vision of the five fires:
we have already stated that the commonality of the fire, fuel, and so forth is for the purpose of praising the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Therefore, the attainment of the path beginning with light does not result from a thorough knowledge of the six categories of topics beginning with departure (*utkrānti*).
"Thus" (evam) refers to the injunction for the attainment of the path beginning with light (arcis), by taking up the subject under discussion.
Who, then, are those who "know thus"? They are indeed householders. But is it not the case that for them, the attainment of smoke and so forth is intended through the means of sacrifice and the like?

No, for even householders who do not possess such [ascetic] qualities are capable of performing sacrifices and other rites; furthermore, because the mendicant and the forest-dweller are included by virtue of their connection to the forest,
and because the practice of the five fires is connected to the duties of a householder.
Therefore, those who practice celibacy (*brahmacārin*) are not understood here [in this context] as being included;

for their entry upon the northern path is established by the authority of the Smṛti: “Of the eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), who followed the northern path of Aryaman, they indeed attained immortality.”

Therefore, those householders who know themselves in this sequence— "I am born from Fire, I am the offspring of Fire"— and thus understand themselves to be of the nature of Fire; and those who are forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*) established in the forest,
being endowed with faith (*śraddhā*), who, having performed their ablutions, meditate upon Truth (*satya*) as Brahman, the Self of Hiraṇyagarbha, and do not meditate upon Faith itself.
They all proceed toward the flame.

As long as householders do not know the science of the five fires or the true Brahman, they— having been offered as the fifth oblation through the sequence of oblations beginning with faith— are born from the fire of woman and, rising up again into this world, become performers of rites such as the *agnihotra*.
By that karma, they return again to the world of the ancestors through the sequence beginning with smoke, and again to this world through the sequence beginning with rain.
Being born again from the fire of the woman and performing karma once more, they revolve again and again in this very manner through coming and going like a water-wheel.
However, when they know thus, being liberated from the rotation of the water-wheel, they attain the light.

"Light" (arcis) does not refer merely to the flame of fire; rather, it refers to the deity presiding over light, who is denoted by the word "light" and is established as a characteristic of the northern path. It is toward her that they proceed.
For wandering mendicants have no direct connection with the flame of fire itself. Therefore, the deity alone, who is denoted by the word "light," is understood here.

Therefore, the day is the deity; since the restriction of the time of death is untenable, the word "day" (ahar) must also refer to the deity alone. For death occurs only upon the exhaustion of one's lifespan.
For it is not possible to restrict the time of death such that one who knows thus must die on the very day;
nor do those who have become *preta*s at night wait for the day, according to another Vedic text: "As quickly as he might direct his mind, so swiftly does he go to the Sun."

Having been carried across by the day as their presiding deity, they reach the presiding deity of the waxing fortnight—that is, the deity of the bright half of the month. Having been carried across by the deity of the bright fortnight, they reach those six months during which the sun, the impeller, moves northward toward the northern quarter; these are the months they reach. Because of the plural number "months," there are six presiding deities of the northern solstice who move in a group. Having been carried across from those months by the deities of the six months, they reach the deity presiding over the world of the gods.
From the world of the gods (*devaloka*), they reach the sun; from the sun, they reach the lightning—that is, the deity presiding over lightning.
Having reached the deity of lightning, a certain person dwelling in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), created by Brahmā through his mind (*mānasa*), comes and leads them to the worlds of Brahmā.
It is understood that the "worlds of Brahmā" are distinguished by the differentiation of lower and higher levels.
Because of the use of the plural number,
and because the gradations of worship are logically consistent;
having been led by that person, they, being supreme— that is, excellent— in those worlds of Brahman, dwell for many supreme years— that is, excellent years— themselves.

The meaning is that they dwell for many kalpas in the realm of Brahmā. For those who have gone to the world of Brahmā, there is no returning again to this saṃsāra, nor is there any coming back here; this is because of the reading in another Vedic recension (śākhā).

If it is argued that the word "here" (iha) refers merely to the general form [of the world], as in the expression "on the day after tomorrow, at the full moon," [the answer is that this does not apply here].
No, because the qualification "here" (iha) would be purposeless.
For if they did not indeed recur, the mention of "here" would be entirely meaningless.

In the case of the statement "on the next day [one performs] the Full Moon sacrifice," since the fact that the Full Moon occurs on the next day is not explicitly stated, it is appropriate to qualify it.

For in that case, since the form of a dog (*śvākṛti*) does not exist as the meaning of the word, the word *śva-* is employed as being entirely devoid of meaning. However, when a qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇaśabda*) has been employed and, upon investigation, its purpose as a qualifier is not perceived, it is appropriate to discard that qualifying word as being meaningless; but this is not the case when the purpose of the qualifier is indeed understood. Therefore, from this [present] conceptualization, a recurrence [of the previous state] is understood. //15//
Now, those who win the worlds by means of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, they pass into the smoke;
from the smoke, into the night.
From the night [it goes] to the waning fortnight;
from the waning fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves southward;
and from those months to the world of the ancestors.
From the world of the fathers they go to the moon.
Having reached the moon, they become food.
There the gods consume them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, "Swell up! Wane away! and so forth.
When that [knowledge] of theirs becomes fully digested, they then emerge into this very space;
from space, into wind;
from wind, into rain.
From rain they reach the earth;
having reached the earth, they become food.
They are then offered again into the fire of man, and from that they are born in the fire of woman.
Those who rise up toward the worlds revolve in this very same way;
but those who do not know these two paths become worms, moths, and whatever is biting.

Now, however, those who do not know thus—those mere performers of ritual action who are knowers only of the six categories of ritual elements connected with the *agnihotra*, such as the departure [of the breath] and so on—they conquer worlds by means of sacrifice, such as the *agnihotra* and others; by means of giving, characterized by the distribution of goods to those begging outside the sacrificial ground; and by means of austerity, performed outside the sacrificial ground, such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, which are distinct from the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and the like.
By the use of the plural "the worlds," it is intended here as well that there is a gradation of results.
They attain the smoke;
just as on the northern path, so too here the deities themselves are denoted by the words "smoke" and so forth.
The meaning is that they reach the deity of smoke. And the nature of these deities as "conveyors" (ātivāhika) is exactly like that [of the preceding ones].

From smoke they go to the night, that is, the deity of night; from there to the deity of the waning fortnight; from there to those specific deities of the six months during which the sun moves toward the southern direction. They reach those particular lunar-month deities.
From the months they go to the world of the fathers (pitṛloka), and from the world of the fathers to the moon.

Having reached the moon, they become food; and while they are there in the form of food, the performers of ritual acts consume them—just as the officiating priests at a sacrifice here on earth consume King Soma with the words, "Swell up! Wane away!"—so do the masters consume those who have reached the moon like servants.

The gods "consume" and "enjoy" [the performers] with the mantra "Swell up! Wane away!"—this is not a mantra for eating; rather, the meaning is that having repeatedly caused them to swell by means of consumption and having caused them to wane, they consume them again and again.
In this way, the gods also, having obtained bodies in the world of Soma, repeatedly provide rest to the performers who have become their instruments, bestowing fruits in accordance with their karma.
For that [offering] is their nourishment, just as the nourishment of Soma is for those who enjoy it; the gods are merely instruments for those performers of action.
When—at which time—that karma characterized by sacrifice, charity, and so forth, which leads to the world of Soma, "passes away"—meaning it reaches its end and becomes exhausted—then [they fall].
Then they attain this very well-known space.

Those waters, denoted by the word "faith," which were offered into the fire of the heavenly world and transformed into the form of Soma— by means of which a watery body was commenced for the enjoyment of the performers of rituals in the world of Soma— those waters dissolve upon the exhaustion of karma, like a lump of snow through contact with the heat of the sun.
Having dissolved, they become subtle, as if having become the element of space; this is what is meant by the statement, "they attain this very space.

Then again, those performers of ritual action, possessing bodies, are led hither and thither by the east wind and other winds while moving through the intermediate space; regarding this, the text says: "from space, to air.
From air, they reach rain.
As it has been said: "They offer King Soma as an oblation into the fire of Parjanya.
Thereupon, having become rain, these [waters] fall upon this earth. Having reached the earth, they become food such as rice, barley, and so forth.
Thus it has been said: "In this world, they offer rain into the fire; from that oblation, food comes into being.
Those [beings] are then offered into the fire of man, having become food, into the shedder of semen.

Then, having become semen, they are offered into the fire of woman; from that they are born as those who rise up toward the world. Rising up toward the world, they perform rituals such as the Agnihotra."
Then, by means of smoke and so forth, they go again and again to the world of Soma and back to this world;
thus these performers of ritual action revolve like a waterwheel, wandering in a cycle—this is the meaning.
They continue in this way until they know Brahman, for the sake of the higher path or immediate liberation.
Thus it has been stated that one transmigrates while desiring.

Now, however, as for those who do not know these two paths—the northern and the southern—meaning they do not practice either knowledge or action for the sake of attaining the northern or the southern path;
what becomes of them?
It is said: they become those worms, moths, and whatever biting, stinging, and gadflies there are.
For such is this miserable course of saṃsāra; for one submerged in it, a further emergence is indeed difficult to attain.
And so says another Vedic text: “These small creatures that return again and again—they are born and they die.”

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that one should, with all one's enthusiasm and according to one's ability, abandon natural actions and knowledge and practice scriptural action or knowledge, which are the means for attaining the southern or northern path.

Thus it has been said: "Indeed, from there it is very difficult to escape; therefore, one should feel aversion [to worldly life]"—from this other Vedic text, the meaning is that one should strive for liberation.
Here too, it is understood that a great effort must be made specifically toward the means for attaining the northern path.
Because it has been stated that "in this very way they revolve," thus all the questions have been resolved.
Starting from "This indeed is the world," the fourth question—"How many offerings does a person consist of? and so forth—has been answered by the first [offering].

The fifth [question], however, concerns the second [stage] as the point of entry for either the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), by means of explaining the instruments for attaining the southern and northern paths.
By that very [explanation], the first [question] also addresses the disagreement regarding fire: "Some reach the flame (*arcis*), while others reach the smoke (*dhūma*).
And the second question concerns the return: "They come to this world by way of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth."
For that very reason, the world is not filled up, because some [beings] attain the state of insects, moths, and so forth; thus, the third question has also been resolved.
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.1:
He who might desire, "May I attain greatness," should, during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the waxing moon, having observed the *upasad* vow for twelve days,
collect all kinds of herbs and fruits in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood— either a shallow cup or a bowl— and having swept around it...

Having smeared [the ground] and kindled the fire, having strewn grass around it and prepared the clarified butter according to the prescribed rite, he mixes the mash under an auspicious constellation and offers it as an oblation: "O Jātavedas, as many gods as dwell within you who strike down the desires of a man, to them I offer this portion; may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with all my desires, svāhā!"
"You who lie across, saying, 'I am the supporter'—you, the one who brings about harmony, I worship with a stream of clarified butter; Svāhā! Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.1.
Regarding the one who might desire [this]:
the course of knowledge and action has been described.
Therein, knowledge is independent, whereas action depends upon the two kinds of wealth—divine and human. Therefore, for the sake of action, wealth must be acquired.
And that [greatness] is to be achieved by a means that does not entail sin; therefore, for the sake of attaining greatness, the rite called *mantha* is commenced.
For when greatness exists, wealth is indeed established as a matter of course.
Thus it is said: "He who should desire," meaning he who desires wealth—that person authorized for ritual action who should so desire.
What [is it]? The meaning is: "May I attain greatness; may I become great.

In that regard, the time for the intended act of churning is specified: during the northward course of the sun (*udagayana*), and within that, since it applies everywhere, during the waxing fortnight, that is, the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).

In that regard, "everywhere" means at every auspicious time (*puṇyāha*) that is favorable to oneself and conducive to the accomplishment of the rite. For twelve days prior to whichever auspicious and favorable day one intends to perform the ritual, starting from that very auspicious day, one observes the *upasad* vow.
The *upasads* are well-known as the vows performed during the *upasads* of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And in that context, the vow consists of subsisting on milk by means of increasing and decreasing the quantity of breast-milk.
Here, however, because that specific ritual action is not brought forward, only the mere act of subsisting on milk—devoid of any specific procedure—is enjoined.

Now, one might object: when the analysis of the compound *upasado vratam* is taken as "the vow of the *upasads*," then everything consisting of the procedural form should be understood; why, then, is it not accepted?
It is said: because the rite belongs to the Smṛti;
for this rite of churning is indeed based on the Smṛti.
But one might object: since it is ordained by Śruti, how can it be considered based on the Smṛti?

This scriptural statement is merely reiterative of what is already established by memory (Smṛti). For if it were directly based on Śruti, there would be a relationship of original and modification (prakṛti-vikāra), and consequently, the modified rite would necessarily adopt the characteristics of the original; however, in this case, there is no such direct scriptural basis.
It is for this very reason that this rite is prescribed to be performed in the domestic fire (āvasathya-agni).
"And all [this] is according to the Smṛti.
This means that having become one who observes the *upasad* vow, he should be one who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*).
In a vessel made of *udumbara* wood—that is, in either a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa*—the specific qualification being that it must be made of *udumbara* wood and shaped like a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa*.
But the conceptualization applies to the *ākāra* (the specific form), not to the state of being an *udumbara*.

In this context, "all herbs" refers to a collection of all herbs as far as possible and according to one's capacity; having gathered all the herbs there, ten types of cultivated plants—such as rice, barley, and so forth, which will be mentioned below—must necessarily be included.
However, there is no fault in taking more than that;
and one should take the fruits of cultivated plants according to availability and according to one's capacity.
The word "iti" is intended to indicate the accumulation of all such gathered provisions.
The meaning is that one should gather all else that is to be gathered.
In this regard, the sequence should be understood as prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras.
The preparation of the ground consists of sweeping and smearing it.
