From the statement "having kindled the fire," it is understood that this refers to the domestic fire (*āvasathya*), because of the singular number and because of the mention of "kindling. Kindling applies only to a fire that is already present.

Having strewn darbha grass around [the fire] according to the procedure for Smārta rites—since this is a Smārta ritual, the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) is adopted—one should prepare the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Then, under a male asterism (*nakṣatra*) associated with a masculine name and conjoined with an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should pour into a cup made of *udumbara* wood, which contains curds, honey, and ghee, a stirred drink (*mantha*) consisting of ground flour of all medicinal herbs and fruits; having thus poured it in, one should stir it with a single stirring-stick.

Having brought [the clarified butter] together and placed it in the center, he offers oblations of ghee at the place for the additional offerings (āvāpasthāna) with a ladle made of Udumbara wood, using these mantras beginning with "yāvanto devāḥ" and so forth. //1//
Having offered an oblation in the fire with the words, "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation in the fire with the words, "To the breath, svāhā! To the most excellent, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with the words, "To speech, svāhā! To the foundation, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with the words, "To the eye, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with the words, "To the ear, svāhā! To the abode, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To the mind, svāhā! To procreation, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To the seed, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words "Svāhā to Agni," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words "Svāhā to Soma," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words "Bhūḥ Svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhuvaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Brahman," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Kṣatra," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Bhūta," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Bhaviṣya, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Viśva, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Sarva, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To Prajāpati, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered two oblations each, beginning with "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash;
he causes the butter smeared on the ladle to flow into the mash.

From this very indication of the vital breath (prāṇa) in the words "to the eldest," "to the best," and so forth, only those who know the vital breath as the eldest, the best, and so on, are entitled to perform this rite.
Having offered each oblation beginning with the words "From semen," he pours the residue into the mash and churns it again with another churning-stick.
Then he touches him, saying: "Thou art whirling; thou art flaming."
You are full; you are firmly established;
you are the single assembly.
You are the *hiṅ* sound;
you are being uttered as the *hiṅ* sound;
you are the *udgītha*.
You are being chanted; you are being proclaimed; you are being responded to.
In the moist you are kindled;
you are pervasive;
you are powerful.
You are food; you are light; you are the conclusion.
"You are the absorber," [he said]. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.4.
Then he touches him with this mantra: "Thou art the revolving one. //4//
Then he lifts it up [with the mantra]: "O Āman, Āman indeed is thine;
for he is the King, the Ruler, the Overlord."
"May he, the lord of kings, make me his sovereign. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.5)
Then he rises and takes him by the hand together with the vessel, saying: "We shall honor thee, for thou art great. Thus [with this mantra]. //5//
Then he sips water [with the mantra]: "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ..."
Honey for the one who follows the cosmic order; the rivers flow with honey;
may the plants be sweet for us.
Bhūḥ! Svāhā!
We meditate upon the splendor of the god;
may the night be honey-sweet, and may the dawn be honey-sweet; may the earthly realm be honey-sweet, and may our father, heaven, be honey-sweet.
Bhuvaḥ Svāhā!
May he who shall impel our thoughts [be so impelled].
May the Lord of the Forest be full of sweetness for us; may the Sun be full of sweetness.
"May the cows be honey-sweet for us;
heaven, svāhā!
He recites the entire Sāvitrī verse as well.

"May I become all this, and may all [beings] be full of sweetness for me; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā! Having finally sipped water and washed his hands, he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east.
In the morning, he worships the sun:
"You are the unique lotus among the quarters."
"May I become the unique white lotus among men. Having returned by the same way he came, he sits behind the fire and mutters the lineage formula (*vaṃśa*).
Then he sips it, that is, he consumes it. With the first foot of the Gāyatrī, with one verse containing the word "honey" (*madhumatī*), and with the first *vyāhṛti*, he sips the first morsel.
Likewise, with the second foot of the Gāyatrī, with the second *madhumatī* verse, and with the second *vyāhṛti*, he sips the second morsel.
Similarly, with the third foot of the Gāyatrī, with the third *madhumatī* verse, and with the third *vyāhṛti*, he sips the third morsel.

Having recited the entire *Sāvitrī* and all the *Madhumatī* verses, and at the end having said, "May I indeed become all this," he offers the whole [oblation] with the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.
Just as that substance is completely finished with four mouthfuls, so should it be measured out beforehand.
Having washed that vessel which was smeared with food, he should drink the remainder silently.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he lies down behind the fire, with his head toward the east.
Having performed the morning twilight devotion, he worships the sun with this mantra: "The one lotus of the quarters.
Having returned by the same way he came, he sits behind the fire and recites the lineage (*vaṃśa*).

Having taught this very [doctrine] to his pupil Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi said: "Even if one were to pour it upon a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout. Having taught this very [doctrine] to his pupil Madhuka Paiṅgya, Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya said: "Even if one were to pour it upon a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout."
"Palāśa leaves," [he said]. BrhUp 6.3.8.

Madhuka Paiṅgya, having taught this very [doctrine] to his pupil Cūla Bhāgavitti, said: "Even if one were to pour it upon a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout. And Cūla Bhāgavitti, having taught this very [doctrine] to his pupil Jānaki Āyaḥsthūṇa, said: "Even if one were to pour it upon a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout."
Jānaki Āyasthūṇa, having told this very same thing to his pupil Satyakāma Jābāla, said: "Even if one were to pour this upon a withered stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.
And Satyakāma Jābāla, having told this very same thing to his pupils, said: "Even if one were to pour this upon a withered stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.
One should not speak of this to anyone who is not a son or a pupil. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.12)

Having taught this very Mantha—beginning with "Uddālaka" and ending with "if one were to sprinkle it on a dry stump, branches would surely spring up and leaves would grow"—to his pupils, Satyakāma Jābāla, who had received it in succession from each teacher starting from Uddālaka, said: "Even if one were to sprinkle it on a dry stump, branches would surely spring up and leaves would grow. Thus spoke the teacher Satyakāma to many pupils.

What else did he say? It is said: "Even if one were to sprinkle this churned mixture, prepared for consumption, upon a withered tree-stump—even one whose life-force has departed—branches, that is, the limbs of the tree, would surely spring up, and leaves, that is, foliage, would grow upon this stump; how much more so, then, would one's desire be fulfilled by this ritual act?"
"This action has a certain fruit"—this is for the purpose of praising action.

Regarding the acquisition of knowledge, there are four sacred seats (*tīrtha*); among them, here, for the acquisition of this "churning" realization (*manthavijñāna*) which includes the vision of the vital breaths (*sapraṇadarśana*), only two sacred seats are authorized: the son and the pupil. (8–12)
It consists of four things made of *udumbara* wood:
a *sruva* ladle made of *udumbara*, a *camasa* cup made of *udumbara*, a fuel-stick (*idhma*) made of *udumbara*, and two churning-sticks made of *udumbara*.
There are ten kinds of cultivated grains:
rice, barley, sesame, beans, small millet, panic seed, wheat, lentils, peas, and vetches. Having ground them, he pours curds, honey, and ghee over them.
He offers an oblation of clarified butter.
It has been explained that "it consists of four udumbara [vessels].
We have stated that there are ten kinds of cultivated grains, meaning that ten types of cultivated grains must be taken as a rule.

To specify which these are, they are enumerated: rice (vrīhi), barley (yava), sesame (tila), beans (māṣa), millet (aṇu), and panic seed (priyaṅgu); the term *aṇu* refers to a certain grain known by that name in some regions.
The *priyaṅgus* are well known; they are referred to by the word *kaṅgu*.
The *khalvās* are *niṣpāvas*, which in common parlance are called *vallas*, *khalakulas*, or *kulatthas*.
Apart from these, one should take all medicinal herbs according to one's ability, as we have already stated, with the exception of those used for sacrificial purposes (*āyājñika*). //13//
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa of the sixth chapter in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Of these beings, the earth is indeed the essence;
of the earth, the waters.
From water come plants;
from plants, flowers;
from flowers, fruits.
From fruits comes man;
from man comes semen. // Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.1 //
"From all its limbs, light was produced," according to another scriptural passage (BrhU). //1//
Then Prajāpati reflected: "Come now, I shall provide a support for him. He created a woman;
having created her, he approached her from below.
Therefore, one should worship the woman below.
He brought forth from himself this pressing-stone facing eastward;
with it he impregnated her.
Since this semen is thus the most essential element of all beings, what indeed could be a suitable receptacle for it? Thus the creator Prajāpati reflected.
Having reflected, he created a woman;
and having created her, he worshipped her—that is, he performed the act known as sexual union, which is called "worship from below" (*adha-upāsana*).
Therefore, one should worship a woman as being beneath oneself, for offspring follow after their superior.

In this regard, he describes the construction of the similarity with the Vājapeya sacrifice: "He brought forth that upward-pointing organ of procreation—which is endowed with excellent movement and serves as his own *grāvan* (pressing-stone) due to its common quality of hardness—toward the female organ; by means of it, he [impregnated] her."
He bestowed prosperity; he brought about a close union. //2//
Of her, the sacrificial altar is the lap; the sacrificial grass is the body hair.
The two skins for pressing are his testicles, kindled in the middle.
Indeed, as great as is the world of one who performs the Vājapeya sacrifice, so great becomes his world.
He who, knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse with these women takes away their merit;
but he who, not knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse with them—his women take away his merit.

"Indeed, knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi said this—meaning, knowing that the act of sexual intercourse called 'adhopahāsa' is identical to the Vājapeya sacrifice—and likewise Nāka Maudgalya and Kumārahārita.

What did they say? It is explained: 'Many are the mortals,' meaning men subject to death; 'those whose way is Brahman' (brahmaṇāyanāḥ) refers to those who are mere nominal Brahmins (brahmabandhus), living by their birth alone."

"Devoid of sense organs" means having disintegrated organs; "devoid of merit" means those whose meritorious actions have vanished; "the ignorant" means those attached to the act of sexual intercourse—this is the meaning.

To show that the act of sexual intercourse is an extreme cause of sin, [the text] asks: "Do they depart from this world, fallen away from the next?"—"Those who, being ignorant, practice this downward laughter. Having performed the *śrīmantha* rite, one should observe the period of the wife's fertile season with celibacy (*brahmacarya*). If, while engaged in this pleasure, one emits semen—whether much or little, whether asleep or awake—it is due to the intensity of passion. (4)
Knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi used to say: "This, indeed, he knows. Knowing this, Nāka Maudgalya used to say: "This, indeed, he knows."

Knowing this, Kumārahārita indeed said: "Many young men of the Brāhmaṇa caste, devoid of sensory power and stripped of their merit, depart from this world, they who, not knowing this, engage in vulgar laughter.
Indeed, much semen is emitted by one whether sleeping or waking.

Indeed, knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi used to say that the act of sexual intercourse—known as *adhopahāsa* (laughing at what is below)—is equivalent to the Vājapeya sacrifice; that is, he knew it to be a complete Vājapeya.
Likewise, Nāka Maudgalya and Kumārahārita said the same.

What they said is stated here: "Many *maryāḥ*—human beings subject to death—who have Brahmins as their *ayana* (refuge), are *brāhmaṇāyanas*; that is to say, they are mere nominal Brahmins who live by their caste alone."

"Powerless" means those whose senses are disintegrated; "devoid of merit" means those who have lost their virtuous deeds; "ignorant" means they are attached to the act of sexual intercourse—this is the meaning.

To show that the act of sexual intercourse is an extreme cause of sin, he asks: "Do these ignorant ones depart from this world, having fallen away from the next? Thus he says: "Those ignorant ones who practice this downward laughter. Having performed the *śrīmantha* rite, one should observe a period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) while awaiting the time for the wife's menses; for if one indulges in passion during this time, whether sleeping or waking, much or little semen may be discharged due to the intensity of desire. (4)
He should touch it, or recite over it the mantra: "That seed of mine which today has fallen upon the earth, which has flowed into the plants, or into the waters— this very seed I take up."
"May my power return to me, may my vigor return, may my fortune return;

may Agni and the sacrificial hearths be restored to their proper places. Having taken [the substance] with his ring finger and thumb, he should wipe it between his breasts or between his eyebrows. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.5)
"He should touch it" means he should address it with a mantra or recite it after;

when he touches it, then with the mantra ending with "that seed I take up" using the ring finger and the thumb, and with the mantra "again me," he should wipe [it] between the eyebrows or between the breasts.
Now, if he should see his own reflection in water, let him address it with the mantra: "In me be splendor, sensory power, glory, wealth, and merit.
For this woman who has removed her soiled clothes is indeed the Fortune of women;
therefore, one should approach and address a glorious woman who has removed her soiled clothes.
Now, if at any time he should see his own reflection in water, there too he should invite her with this mantra: "May splendor be in me.

For she is indeed Śrī (Prosperity), the consort among women; since she is *malodvāsas*—one whose garments are free from impurity—he should approach that illustrious and prosperous woman and invite her, thinking: "This task must be performed by the two of us today."
Regarding the production of a son: [he should approach] her who has bathed at the end of three nights.
If she should not give it to him, he may, if he wishes, buy her from her;
if she should still not give it to him, he may, if he wishes, strike her with a stick or with his hand and pass beyond her.
"By means of your faculty, I take away your fame"—thus he becomes indeed devoid of fame. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.4.7.
If she does not grant him sexual intercourse for the purpose of procreating a son, he should inform her at the end of three nights.

Even if she still does not grant it, he may, if he so desires, strike her with a stick or with his hand and pass her by for the sake of sexual intercourse, proclaiming, "I shall curse you; I shall make you unfortunate. Having done so, he should approach her with this mantra: "By my organ, by my glory, I take away your glory."
On account of that curse, she became known as barren and unfortunate, and indeed remained ill-reputed. //7//
If she should give it to him, he should say: "With my faculty, with my glory, I bestow glory upon you. Thus both become glorious. BrhUp 6.4.8.

If she should give it to him, it would be entirely suitable for the husband; then he should approach her with this mantra: "With my organ, with glory, I bestow glory upon you. Then both of them indeed become glorious. //8//
If he should desire her—thinking, "May she love me"—he should place his purpose in her, join mouth to mouth, touch her private parts, and mutter:
"From limb by limb you arise; from the heart you are born."
Therefore, you are one whose limbs are smeared with poison; intoxicate this woman here for me, as if she were pierced by a poisoned arrow.

If he should desire his wife, thinking, "May she love me," he should fix his organ—the instrument of procreation—within her, join mouth to mouth, touch her private parts, and mutter this mantra: "From limb by limb... (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.9).
Now, if he should desire of her, "May she not conceive," he should, after depositing his semen in her, join mouth to mouth and, having breathed in, breathe out [upon her],
saying: "By my organ, with my seed, I take back your seed."
He indeed becomes one who possesses heroic power. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.10.
Now, if one should desire that she not conceive—that she should not become pregnant—the procedure is as before:

having first performed inhalation (*abhiprāṇya*), he should afterwards exhale with this mantra, "By my organ and seed, I take away your seed. The meaning is that she becomes seedless; she does not become pregnant.

Now, if he should desire of a woman, "May she conceive," having performed the ritual act upon her, joining mouth to mouth, he should exhale and then inhale, saying: "With my faculty and with my seed, I place seed in you.
She indeed becomes pregnant.
Now, if one should desire, "May she conceive a fetus," he should perform the rite as before, beginning with the words, "I place the seed in her.
However, he should do so by reversing the previous order: exhaling and then inhaling, saying, "By means of my organ and my seed, I place seed in yours. Thus she indeed becomes pregnant. //11//
Now, if one should hate a man who has a lover for his wife, he should kindle a fire in an unbaked earthen vessel, spread out sacrificial grass with its points turned away [from the fire],
and into that [fire] he should offer these arrow-heads, smeared with clarified butter, with their points turned away.
"You have offered in my kindled fire! I take away your out-breath and in-breath, O So-and-so! "You have offered in my kindled fire!"
"I take away your sons and cattle, O so-and-so! "You have offered [the oblation] into my well-kindled fire. "I take away your sacrifices and good deeds, O so-and-so!"
"You have sacrificed in my consecrated fire!
I take away your heaven and space, O so-and-so!"—
indeed, he whom a Brahmin knowing this curses departs from this world deprived of his senses and stripped of his merit.
Therefore, one who knows this should not seek to joke with the wife of a learned Śrotriya;
for indeed, one who knows this becomes superior.
Now, furthermore, if one should have a paramour or lover for his wife, and he should hate him and think, "I will practice sorcery against him," this is the ritual for him:

having kindled a fire in an unbaked clay vessel, he should perform everything in a reverse order; in that fire, he should offer as oblations these reed-shafts—the stalks of reeds in a reverse order, smeared with ghee—that is, anointed with clarified butter, saying at the end: "In my well-kindled fire you have offered," and so forth.
The mention of the name "asau" (so-and-so) is for each of them individually.
A Brahmin who possesses such knowledge, when he pronounces a curse, departs from this world having lost his merit—that is, his virtuous karma.

Therefore, one who knows this should not desire to joke with the wife of a learned Śrotriya, nor should he even engage in playful banter, much less in malicious mockery; for even such a person as this remains a stranger, meaning he remains an enemy.
Now, if one should find his wife in her menses, she shall not drink from a bronze vessel for three days,
nor wear unwashed garments.
Neither a Śūdra nor a Śūdra woman shall thresh this [grain].
At the end of three nights, having bathed, one should have the rice threshed.

Now, the passage beginning with "If one should find his wife in her menses" and ending with "she indeed is the prosperity of women" should be seen as occurring prior to that [section]. By implication, she should drink [water] from a bronze vessel for three days and remain in unwashed clothes. Neither a *vṛṣala* nor a *vṛṣalī* should defile her—meaning they should not touch her—whether she has bathed or not.

"At the end of the three nights," meaning upon the completion of the vow of three nights, "having bathed" (āplutya) and being dressed in unwashed garments—this is the connection with the distant [word].
"One should cause her, having thus bathed, to thresh the rice"; that is, one should employ her specifically for the purpose of threshing the rice. //13//

If one should desire: "May a fair son be born to me; may he recite the Veda; may he live his full span of life," then, having cooked rice with milk, they two should eat it with clarified butter. They are capable of procreating. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.14)

If one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is fair in complexion, who may recite a single Veda, and who may live the full span of life—hundred years"—then, having cooked milk-rice with clarified butter, the two of them should eat it; they will be capable of procreating, indeed, capable of procreating.

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is tawny and reddish-brown, who shall master two Vedas, and who shall live his full span of life," they should have curd-rice cooked with clarified butter and eat it; thus they will be capable of procreating such a child. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.15)
If he desires a son who will be devoted to two deities, he should cook a *caru* of rice with curd; such is the rule regarding the food. 15.

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is dark-complexioned and red-eyed, who shall master the three Vedas and live his full span of life," then, having cooked rice with milk, they both should eat it with clarified butter; thus they will be able to procreate. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.16)
The mention of "rice" alone is intended to indicate that it is purely natural, for the purpose of precluding any connection with other [kinds of food]. //16//

Now, if one should desire, "May a learned daughter be born to me; may she live her full span of life," they should have rice cooked with sesame seeds and eat it with clarified butter. They will thus be capable of procreating [such a child]. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.17)
The daughter's scholarship pertained only to the management of the household, as she lacked authority over the Veda; she had prepared rice mixed with sesame seeds. //17//

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is wise, renowned, capable in assembly, able to speak with eloquence when questioned, who shall master all the Vedas and live his full span of life," then, having had rice cooked with meat,
they two should eat it with clarified butter.
The two lords should cause [the fire] to be generated by means of a bull or a steer. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.18.
"Vigīta" means variously sung; that is to say, well-known.
"Samitiṅgamaḥ" means one who goes to an assembly; that is to say, bold, since "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship) has been mentioned separately.
"Desired speech" means speech that is pleasant to hear and beautiful; "spoken" means spoken in a refined and meaningful language. "Meat-rice" (māṃsaudana) refers to rice mixed with meat.
To specify the type of meat, he says: "or beef (aukṣa) with meat."
An *ukṣan* is a bull capable of mating; its meat is *aukṣam*. An *ṛṣabha* is one even older than that; its meat is *ārṣabham*. //17//

Then, at the very break of dawn, having performed the ritual with clarified butter according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*, he offers a portion of the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Anumati, svāhā! To the god Savitṛ of true impulsion, svāhā!
Having offered it and taken out [the remainder], he eats it.
He eats [the remainder] and gives it to the other woman.
Having washed his hands and filled a water-vessel, he sprinkles her with it three times, saying: "Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu; seek another woman who is more favorable."
"May he be united with his wife," so [he says]. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.4.19.

Then, at the very time of dawn, having taken the rice grains that have been prepared by threshing, and having performed the rites for the *sthālīpāka*—that is, having carried out the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*, prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—he offers oblations of the *sthālīpāka* by taking portions repeatedly, saying "To Agni, Svāhā! and so forth.
All the domestic (*gārhya*) rules are to be observed here. Having offered the oblations and drawn out the remainder of the porridge, he eats it himself; he gives the leftovers to his wife.

Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he fills a water-vessel and sprinkles her three times with that water while reciting this mantra; the mantra is uttered only once. //19//
Then he approaches her, saying: "I am he (ama), you are she (sā);
you are she, I am he."
I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc;
I am heaven, you are earth. Come, let us two join together; let us both deposit the seed.
"For a man, for sons, for wealth. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.20)

Then, having consecrated her with a mantra and eaten rice cooked in milk and other foods according to his desire for offspring—this is the sequence to be understood—he approaches her at the time of union with the mantra beginning, "I am he (Amaḥ). //20//
Then he causes her thighs to be spread apart, saying: "May you two, Heaven and Earth, open yourselves.
Having positioned himself upon her and joining his mouth to her mouth, he strokes her three times in the direction of the hair.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms.
May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O Pṛthuṣṭukī, bestow an embryo.
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow the embryo upon you.
Then he causes her thighs to be spread apart with the mantra, "May you two, Heaven and Earth, open yourselves.
Regarding her, the ritual procedure beginning with "the purpose" (tasyām artham) is as before.
He strokes her three times from the head downwards in the direction of the hair, reciting the mantras beginning with "Viṣṇu has prepared the womb" for each.
The two golden fire-drills with which the Aśvins churned [the fire]—
with those we invoke this embryo of yours for birth in the tenth month.
"As the earth contains fire within it, as the sky is pregnant with Indra, and as the wind is the embryo of the quarters, so do I place an embryo in you, O [Name]! (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22)
At the end, one utters her name, saying "So-and-so. This is the rule for that [offering]. //22//
When she is about to give birth, he sprinkles her with water:
"As the wind agitates a lotus pond on every side."
"Thus let your embryo stir; let it come forth together with the afterbirth.
This stall for Indra has been prepared, secured with a bolt and surrounded by a fence.
O Indra, drive that [embryo] out with the fetus, along with the afterbirth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.23)
When she is about to give birth, he sprinkles her with water at the time of delivery for the sake of an easy birth with this mantra:
"Just as the wind agitates a lotus pond on all sides, so may your embryo stir. (23)

When [the son] is born, having kindled the fire, placed him on his lap, and poured clotted butter into a bronze vessel, he offers oblations of clotted butter, dipping it into the vessel, with the mantra:
"May I thrive in this man, prospering in my own house; may a thousandfold prosperity attend me."
May he not cut me off from this lap [of the earth] regarding offspring and cattle, svāhā!
I offer my vital breaths into you with my mind, svāhā! Whatever I have overdone in this rite, or whatever I have done here deficiently—
May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make our sacrifice well-sacrificed and well-offered; Svāhā!

Now follows the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). When [the son] is born, having kindled the fire and placed the son on his lap, he mixes speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)—consisting of curds and ghee—in a bronze vessel; then, taking portions of that speckled butter, he offers oblations with the mantra beginning "In this [son], a thousandfold... and so forth, at the place for the insertion of mantras.
Then, placing [his mouth] close to his right ear, he says "Speech! Speech! three times.
Then, having mixed together curds, honey, and ghee, he makes him eat it with a piece of gold that is not separated from it, saying:
"I place *bhūḥ* in you; I place *bhuvaḥ* in you; I place *svaḥ* in you; *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, I place everything in you."
Then, having placed his own mouth close to the boy's right ear, he should whisper three times, "Speech! Speech!

Then, having mixed together curd, honey, and ghee, he should have him eat it with a piece of gold that is not separated from or covered by anything else, using these mantras for each ingredient individually.
Then he gives him a name, saying, "You are Veda. This becomes his secret name indeed.
Then he gives him a name with the words, "Thou art Veda. That becomes his secret name, namely "Veda."

Then, having handed him over to his mother, he gives her the breast, saying: "O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, which bestows jewels, which finds wealth, which is a good giver, and by which you nourish all desirable things—that, I place here for him to suck. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.27)
Then, having handed him over to his mother, she gives him her breast while he is held on her lap, with the mantra beginning, "That breast of yours... (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.27).
Then he addresses his mother: "Thou art Ilā, daughter of Mitra and Varuṇa; thou hast brought forth a hero from a hero.
Mayest thou become possessed of heroes, she who has made us possessed of heroes."
Regarding him, they say: "Truly, you have become a great-grandfather!
Truly, you have become a great-great-grandfather!
You have indeed reached the highest pinnacle in prosperity, fame, and the splendor of sacred knowledge."
"Only the son of a Brahmin who knows this is truly born," so it is said.

Then he addresses his mother with the mantra, "Thou art Ilā," according to this rule: "The son thus born surpasses his father and grandfather in prosperity, fame, and spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa)," meaning that he becomes worthy of praise by attaining the highest perfection.
And for that Brāhmaṇa who knows thus, if a son is born, he also becomes such—this is to be supplied [to the text]. //28//
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the sixth Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.1–4 Now, the lineage: Pautimāṣīputra [received it] from Kātyāyanīputra.
